literary-lapses: Canadian humorist Stephen Leacock packs this book with short comic sketches that made him one of the most beloved funny writers of his time. He pokes gentle fun at boarding houses, college life, insurance salesmen, and the small absurdities of everyday living. The pieces are brief, clever, and warm — classic Leacock, and a fine introduction to a master of the light comic essay.
amanda-a-daughter-of-the-mennonites: Anna Balmer Myers sets her novel among the Mennonite farms of Pennsylvania Dutch country, where young Amanda grows up between two worlds. Plain dress and strict faith shape her daily life, but her heart pulls toward the wider world beyond the fields. Myers, who knew the community well, writes a tender romance about tradition, family duty, and a young woman choosing her own path.
two-years-in-the-french-west-indies: Lafcadio Hearn, the writer who later became famous for his books on Japan, spent two years in Martinique in the 1880s. These sketches capture Creole markets, voodoo-tinged folklore, tropical storms, and the slow rhythms of island life. Hearn writes with a poet's ear for color and sound, preserving a Caribbean world on the edge of change.
a-brief-history-of-the-united-states: Joel Dorman Steele's compact textbook carried generations of American schoolchildren from Columbus to the modern age. Clear timelines, memorable stories, and review questions made it a classroom staple of the late 1800s. Though its view of history is dated, the book remains an interesting record of how young Americans were once taught their country's story.
short-cruises: W. W. Jacobs, remembered today for the chilling Monkey's Paw, was equally loved for his comic tales of sailors and dockside life. This collection gathers short voyages full of bungling seamen, sharp-tongued wives, and practical jokes gone wrong. Jacobs's dry, salty humor made him one of England's most popular storytellers.
the-new-boy-at-hilltop-and-other-stories: Ralph Henry Barbour, the beloved chronicler of schoolboy sports, gathers tales of the new boy finding his place at Hilltop School. Football fields, dormitory friendships, and tests of character fill these warm, clean stories. Barbour understood boy life like few others, and his books were the treasured companions of generations of young readers.
the-pretentious-young-ladies: Molière's sparkling 1659 comedy mocks two young women who put on ridiculous airs of refinement, and the clever servants who trick them. Les Précieuses ridicules made the young playwright's name in Paris with its devastating wit. In this translation, English readers can enjoy one of the funniest satires on social climbing ever written.
the-junior-classics-volume-6-old-fashion: The sixth Junior Classic gathers old-fashioned tales — the gentle, moral stories that grandparents remembered from their own childhoods. William Patten chose pieces meant to be read aloud by the fireside, full of kindness and simple virtue. For modern readers, the volume is a lovely window into what children were once given to cherish.
tom-slade-boy-scout-of-the-moving-pictur: Percy Fitzhugh's sturdy hero Tom Slade gets mixed up with the movies in this installment of the beloved series. When motion-picture men come to town, the scouts find adventure both in front of and behind the camera. A fun period piece from the days when films themselves were still a novelty.
owindia-a-true-tale-of-the-mackenzie-riv: Charlotte Bompas, wife of an Anglican bishop in the far north, tells the true story of Owindia and the Mackenzie River peoples she came to know. Her account mixes missionary purpose with genuine affection for Indigenous life in the subarctic. A rare woman's voice from the nineteenth-century Canadian frontier.
in-midsummer-days-and-other-tales: August Strindberg — the great Swedish dramatist — shows his mastery of the short story in this collection. Tales of midsummer light and shadow explore love, nature, and the mysteries of the human heart. Though best known for his fierce plays, Strindberg's stories reveal a tender, observant artist.
the-adventures-of-sir-launcelot-greaves: Smollett's most lighthearted novel sends Sir Launcelot Greaves — an English Don Quixote in armor — riding out to right wrongs and rescue damsels. His comic tilts at modern windmills delighted eighteenth-century readers. A merry, good-natured romp from the usually sardonic Smollett.
mogens-and-other-stories: J. P. Jacobsen — Denmark's great nineteenth-century storyteller — gathers tales of passion and fate in this collection. The title story follows Mogens through love and loss with a naturalist's eye for human nature. Jacobsen's sensuous, melancholy prose made him a master of the European short story.
the-man-upstairs-and-other-stories: Wodehouse gathers early short stories — comic, romantic, and sporting — showing the young master finding his voice. The title story and its companions offer laughs in the unmistakable Wodehouse manner, lighter than his later Jeeves tales but full of promise. A treat for devotees and newcomers alike.
pickle-the-spy-or-the-incognito-of-princ: Andrew Lang — better known for his fairy books — turns historian to unmask Pickle the Spy, the traitor who betrayed Bonnie Prince Charlie's Jacobite circle. Drawing on secret correspondence, Lang names the spy and tells the full story of the Young Pretender's hidden years. History as detective work, by a master storyteller.
average-jones: Samuel Hopkins Adams introduces Average Jones, a plain young man with a rare gift for solving crimes, mostly through small ads in the papers. His cases are smart, his ways are new, and his modesty is winning. A fresh and most enjoyable twist on the detective tale.
canada-and-the-states: Sir Edward Watkin — the railway magnate behind the Channel Tunnel's first attempt — writes on Canada's relations with the United States and Britain. His letters and speeches argue for closer imperial ties and the railways to bind them. A revealing look at Victorian visions of empire, commerce, and the Canadian future.
the-majesty-of-calmness-individual-probl: William George Jordan's beloved essays preach the power of calmness — the quiet strength that masters life's problems and steadies the mind. His gentle, aphoristic wisdom made this 1898 book a classic of inspirational literature. Readers seeking serenity will find a wise and soothing companion.
the-gerrard-street-mystery-and-other-wei: John Charles Dent — the Canadian historian — tries his hand at the supernatural in this collection of weird tales. The title mystery and its companions offer proper Victorian chills in a colonial setting. An unusual and entertaining sideline from a serious scholar.
in-divers-tones: Sir Charles G. D. Roberts — the father of Canadian poetry — gathers lyrics in divers tones, from nature and love to patriotism. His musical verse helped give the young Dominion a literature of its own. A graceful collection from a major and much-loved voice.
tomaso-s-fortune-and-other-stories: Henry Seton Merriman, prince of the romantic tale of adventure, offers stories of sought and won fortunes in far lands. Title tale and mates alike are trim, tense, and touched with love. Capital reading from a master too seldom praised.
made-over-dishes: S. T. Rorer's thrifty cookbook shows how to make over leftovers into delicious new dishes — economy raised to culinary art. Practical wisdom for household managers of the 1900s, with tested recipes throughout. Waste not, want not, deliciously. Her practical chapters turn thrift into a genuine household art.
a-hive-of-busy-bees: Effie Mae Williams offers young readers a hive of busy bees — short tales, verses, and lessons on kindness, work, and good cheer. Written for children learning to read and to be good. A sweet, old-fashioned book of simple virtues.
david-poindexter-s-disappearance-and-oth: Julian Hawthorne, the romancer's son, offers tales of mystery headed by the strange vanishing of David Poindexter. His stories blend the supernatural with the psychological, in his father's haunting manner but with his own touch. Good, eerie reading for all lovers of the uncanny and unexplained.
the-magnificent-lovers-les-amants-magnif: Molière's courtly comedy-ballet, written for the pleasures of Louis XIV, celebrates magnificent lovers amid music, dance, and spectacle. A rare glimpse of the great playwright as royal entertainer, crafting delight for a king. Graceful, gallant, and very French in spirit.
specimens-of-greek-tragedy-aeschylus-and: Chosen scenes from Aeschylus and Sophocles bring the grandeur of Greek tragedy to English readers. Kings, gods, and relentless fate move through these mighty specimens — the Agamemnon, Oedipus, and Antigone in their power. The foundation stones of all Western drama.
une-vie-a-piece-of-string-and-other-stor: Maupassant's great novel Une Vie — the life of a Norman woman worn down by marriage — joins his perfect short stories, including the immortal Piece of String. The master's clear, pitiless eye is everywhere. French realism at its peak. Jeanne's life, from bright hopes to quiet ruin, is told with Maupassant's unmatched clarity.
knock-knock-knock-and-other-stories: Turgenev's shorter tales — including the eerie Knock, Knock, Knock — show the Russian master's range beyond his great novels. Ghosts, huntsmen, and human hearts fill these pages. Exquisite storytelling in miniature. Hunts, hauntings, and the Russian soul fill these brief, perfect tales.
indian-fairy-tales: Joseph Jacobs gathers the fairy tales of India — clever jackals, brave princes, and magical transformations — retold with charm. His collection opened the riches of Indian folklore to English children. Stories as bright as jewels. Tigers, princes, and clever maidens dance through these sparkling Eastern stories.
suburban-sketches: William Dean Howells sketches suburban life — the streetcars, the neighbors, the small dramas of the American suburb. His quiet humor and keen eye elevate the everyday. A gentle classic of American realism. His delicate wit finds the poetry hiding in commuter trains and front porches.
elder-conklin-and-other-stories: Frank Harris gathers stories headed by Elder Conklin — tales of the American West and the Old World, told with his notorious gusto. His vivid, headlong narratives divide readers still. A racy collection from a racy writer. Cowboys, preachers, and wanderers fill these bold tales, told in Harris's unmistakable voice.
the-principal-navigations-voyages-traffi: Richard Hakluyt's mighty collection continues — the voyages, traffics, and discoveries of the English nation in the age of Elizabeth. Drake, Hawkins, and Frobisher sail again in these pages. The prose epic of England's sea dogs. Storms, savages, and sea fights crowd his immortal pages.
seven-english-cities: William Dean Howells tours seven English cities — their streets, people, and character — with his usual gentle penetration. An American abroad at his most observant. Charming travel sketches from a master. Cathedrals, markets, and quiet squares pass before his kindly American eye.
memories-of-canada-and-scotland-speeches: The Duke of Argyll, once Governor General of Canada, gathers speeches and verses on the lands he loved — Canada and Scotland. His memories bridge the old world and the new. A stateman's affectionate tribute. Rideau Hall days and Highland moors mingle in this nobleman's fond recollections.
cambridge-sketches: Frank Preston Stearns sketches Cambridge, Massachusetts — its scholars, poets, and eccentrics in the golden age of Harvard. Longfellow, Lowell, and their circle live in these affectionate pages. A fond portrait of America's Athens. Elm-shaded streets and famous firesides glow in his nostalgic prose.
autobiographic-sketches: De Quincey turns to his own life in these autobiographic sketches — childhood, schooldays, and the making of the opium-eater. His extraordinary memory and style transform the personal into the universal. Essential for all admirers of a unique genius. Lake District wanderings and London fogs both glow in his opium-tinted prose.
three-comedies: Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson, Norway's Nobel laureate, offers three comedies — witty plays of love and society. His dramatic genius shines beyond the serious works. Delightful Scandinavian theater. Peasants, pastors, and lovers people his humane northern stage. Bjornson's people laugh, love, and learn in these lively plays.
lifted-masks-stories: Susan Glaspell's Lifted Masks gathers stories of women unmasking truth — her keen, compassionate tales of Midwestern life. The great dramatist's fiction deserves wider fame. Powerful, perceptive stories. Her women confront convention with quiet, steely courage. Glaspell's insight into women's hearts never falters.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol: Verses from the Oldest Portfolio gathers Holmes' last gleanings — unpublished and late poems of his great old age. The final flowers of a long and honored literary life, gathered with loving care. A touching farewell volume. Even the fragments show the master's touch undimmed.
a-peep-behind-the-scenes: Mrs. O. F. Walton's Peep Behind the Scenes — the story of a poor theater child — moved Victorian England to tears by the thousand. Her evangelical tale of suffering and salvation became an enormous bestseller. Simple pathos that touched millions of hearts.
friends-in-council-first-series: Arthur Helps' Friends in Council — imaginary conversations among friends on life's great questions — charmed Victorian readers on both sides of the sea. His gentle wisdom made philosophy sociable and delightful. A classic of fireside thought, still worth an evening. Ellesmere, Dunsford, and Milverton debate with urbane good humor.
english-fairy-tales: Joseph Jacobs collects the true English fairy tales — Jack and the Beanstalk, the Three Bears, Tom-Tit-Tot, and all the old favorites — with scholarly notes on their history. The definitive collection of England's folk stories. Every nursery should hold it.
the-man-with-two-left-feet-and-other-sto: Wodehouse gathers stories of the Man with Two Left Feet and other comic unfortunates — tales of love, blunder, and London life. The master's early short fiction at its most infectious and light-hearted. Laughter on every page, guaranteed. Bertie Wooster's cousins stumble through love in these early gems.
the-huge-hunter-or-the-steam-man-of-the-: Edward Ellis' Huge Hunter introduces the Steam Man of the Prairies — a giant steam-powered robot that hunts buffalo across the plains. Published in 1868, this dime novel gave science fiction one of its very first robots. Boys thrilled to the mechanical marvel and its boy inventor. A landmark of early American science fiction, crude but delightful.
half-past-seven-stories: Robert Gordon Anderson's Half-Past Seven Stories are bedtime tales for children, told with gentle fancy and warm humor. His story-hour favorites — of toys, animals, and small wonders — delighted young listeners. Parents will find them perfect for reading aloud. A sweet collection for the nursery shelf.
the-glory-of-the-trenches: Coningsby Dawson's Glory of the Trenches gathers letters and sketches from the Western Front of the Great War. His earnest prose bears witness to horror, comradeship, and sacrifice. The book honors the men who fought and fell. A moving wartime memoir of 1918.
the-nomad-of-the-nine-lives: Abby Frances Friebe's Nomad of the Nine Lives follows a cat through nine adventurous lives — alley, farm, and fireside by turns. Her feline hero's escapades, told with humor and heart, charm every page. Young animal lovers will adore this whiskered wanderer. A purr-fect children's tale.
crucial-instances: Edith Wharton's Crucial Instances gathers stories of turning points in well-bred lives — each tale pivoting on a moment of moral choice. Her ironic mastery and perfect sentences shine throughout. These are Wharton's short fiction at its very finest. Unmissable for her admirers.
more-jataka-tales: Ellen Babbitt's More Jataka Tales continues her beloved retellings of the Buddha's former lives — talking animals teaching gentle morals. Each story is short, wise, and kind. Children love them, and storytellers treasure them. A classic collection of Eastern wisdom. Wise hares, kind elephants, and clever monkeys teach without preaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-ferr: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Ferrières, the old monks' house in the Gâtinais. Its great glory was Lupus, the learned abbot of the ninth century. Henri Leclercq tells the house's long tale. Letters and books were its pride. His letters to popes and kings survive as models of Latin style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-st-s: The Encyclopedia's Solesmes entry: the house that brought back Gregorian chant. Dom Guéranger's monks sang the old songs anew. George Cyprian Alston honors the revival. Plainchant's modern home. Its monks' chant recordings circle the globe today. Its liturgical books guide choirs worldwide.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abipones: A 1913 entry on the Abipones — the fierce Argentine tribe tamed by Jesuit missions. Adolph Bandelier draws on Dobrizhoffer's classic account. Horsemen of the Chaco, they met a tragic end. A moving chapter of mission history. Dobrizhoffer's book remains the classic on their fate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abrahamites: A 1913 entry on the Abrahamites — the Bohemian sect that owned no creed but the Lord's Prayer. John Joseph A'Becket tells their odd story. Joseph II deported the stubborn remnant. Reason's children, lost in the Enlightenment. Their chapel at Lhota kept the old plain ways.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acts-of-the-a: A 1913 entry on the Acts of the Apostles — Luke's history of the infant Church. A.E. Breen covers author, date, and truth. Pentecost to Paul's Roman prison, in twenty-eight chapters. The Church's own first history. Luke's we-passages mark his own journeys. The book ends with Paul still preaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adamites: A 1913 entry on the Adamites — the sects that aped Eden's nakedness. Francis Havey traces their strange story. Bohemian fanatics revived the folly. The Church condemned their paradise. Heresy in search of innocence. Their last sects died in the eighteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-admiral-sands: A 1913 entry on Admirals Benjamin and James Sands — the American naval officers. Thomas Meehan records their service. Their careers spanned the Civil War era. The entry honors Catholic sailors. The Navy's Catholic sons. Their swords rest in the naval museum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aguas-calient: A 1913 entry on Aguas Calientes — the Mexican diocese of the hot waters. John Joseph A'Becket gives its story. Its churches rose on the colonial plain. The faith took root in New Spain. A young see of old Mexico. Its fairs draw the whole Bajio region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albanenses: This 1913 reference article on the Albanenses — a branch of the Cathar heretics. Francis Grey notes their Italian haunts. Their dualism denied the good creation. The Church's inquisitors pursued them. A sect of the medieval shadows. Their stronghold fell to the crusaders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albigenses: A 1913 entry on the Albigenses — the Cathar heretics of southern France. Nicholas Weber tells their tragic tale. Their dualism denied the good creation. Simon de Montfort crushed them in war. The Church's sternest medieval trial. Their castles dot the Languedoc hills.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-of-: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Alexander of Hales — the Franciscan doctor irrefragabilis. William Turner honors his great Summa. He brought Aristotle to the friars' schools. Paris hailed his teaching. Theology's English founder. His Summa filled the friars' libraries. Bonaventure learned at his feet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandre-de-: A 1913 entry on Alexandre de Rhodes — the Jesuit apostle of Vietnam. Nicholas Weber honors his labors. His romanized script taught a nation. Persecution could not stop him. The father of Vietnamese letters. His dictionary opened Vietnam to Europe. His catechism taught a million converts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfonso-de-va: This 1913 reference article on Alfonso de Valdés — the Spanish humanist of Charles V's court. Klemens Löffler sketches his Erasmian mind. His dialogues mocked the Roman court. The emperor prized his pen. A reformer who stayed Catholic. His death cut short a bright career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-breadbo: A 1913 entry on altar breadboxes — the vessels that keep the hosts. Augustin Schulte details their form. Their lids guard the sacred bread. Sacristies treasure the best. Humble keepers of the holy. Their silver shines in the old sacristies. Their craft shows the goldsmith's art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-candles: A 1913 entry on altar candles — the lights of the sanctuary. Augustin Schulte sets out their number and use. Beeswax burns for the Blessed Sacrament. Their flames mean Christ the light. The altar's shining servants. Their smoke rises like the psalmist's prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altars-in-the: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on altars in the Greek churches — the Byzantine holy table. Andrew Shipman describes its veiled splendor. The iconostasis hides it from the nave. Only priests pass the royal doors. The East's holy of holies. Its veil opens at the consecration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amazones: This 1913 reference piece on the Amazons — the legendary warrior women. The entry notes their place in old tales. Greeks set them at the world's edge. Their legend colored ancient art. Myth's fierce sisterhood. Their girdles were heroes' prizes. Their queen fell to Achilles' spear.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosio-mora: This 1913 reference piece on Ambrosio Morales — the Spanish humanist historian. Jeremiah Ford honors his chronicles. His Antiquities lit old Iberia. Philip II valued his learning. A scholar of Spain's golden age. His chronicle ends with the Goths. His volumes grace the Escorial.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-american-fede: This 1913 reference piece on the American Federation of Catholic Societies — the laymen's great union — tells its work. Andrew MacErlean wrote it up. It gave the laity one strong voice. A hundred groups marched as one. Its yearly meets drew great crowds. The Church's lay army, in rank and file.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ammonites: This 1913 reference piece on the Ammonites — Lot's descendants east of Jordan. John Francis Fenlon tells their story. Rabbah's crown came to David. Their wars fill the old books. Israel's eastern neighbors. Their god Moloch demanded cruel rites. Their capital Rabbah fell to Joab.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amorrhites: A 1913 entry on the Amorrhites — the Amorites of the old Canaan. John Francis Fenlon tells their story. Their kings faced Joshua's armies. The Bible remembers their high places. A people of the conquest. Their cities fell to Israel's sword. Their name means the highlanders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anchorites: This 1913 reference piece on anchorites — the walled-up hermits of old England. James Loughlin tells their austere life. Julian of Norwich wrote in her cell. Their windows opened on the church. Prayer behind stone walls. Their cells adjoined the parish church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-of-rho: A 1913 entry on Andrew of Rhodes — the Greek theologian of the union council. John Finnerty notes his part. He argued for East-West reunion. Florence heard his learned voice. A bridge between the churches. His speech moved the Latin fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angels-of-the: This 1913 reference piece on the Angels of the Churches — the seven of the Apocalypse. Hugh Pope weighs their meaning. Bishops or guardians, scholars debate. The letters warn and console. Revelation's mysterious watchers. Their lamps burn before the throne. Their meaning still divides the learned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-annates: This 1913 reference article on annates — the first fruits paid to Rome. Johann Peter Kirsch traces their history. Benefices rendered their first year's fruit. Kings and popes quarreled over them. The old tax of the papal court. Their abolition eased the German church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antidicomaria: A 1913 entry on the Antidicomarianites — the deniers of Mary's perpetual virginity. Andrew Shipman notes the old heresy. St. Epiphanius refuted their error. The Church guards the Mother's honor. A vanished sect of the fourth century. Their error died with the sect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antipodes: This 1913 reference article on the antipodes — the men beneath our feet. James Loughlin traces the old debate. The medievals argued their existence. The Church never condemned the globe. Geography's ancient puzzle. Their discovery vindicated the old globe. Their sailors proved the scholars right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-da-fo: This 1913 reference article on Antonio da Fonseca Soares — a Franciscan of note. Stephen Donovan records his career. The entry preserves his modest fame. His order honors its learned sons. A friar among the writers. His sermons edified the Portuguese faithful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apaches: This 1913 reference article on the Apaches — the missions among the raiders. William Fanning tells the hard story. The friars followed the wandering bands. The frontier tested their courage. The Church's hardest mission field. Their raids tested the presidio soldiers. Their language baffled the interpreters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apelles: This 1913 reference piece on Apelles — the Marcionite heretic. John Bertram Peterson notes his errors. He softened his master's harsh creed. The Fathers refuted his fancies. A heretic of the second century. His Philumene claimed angelic visions. His gospel twisted the true text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aphraates: A 1913 entry on Aphraates — the Persian Sage of the Syriac Church. Francis Albert honors his Demonstrations. His homilies are the oldest Syriac prose. The Persian Church prized his wisdom. The sage beyond the Empire. His homilies number twenty-three. His Syriac is the scholars' delight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostles: This 1913 reference article on the Apostles — the Twelve chosen by Christ. Honoré Coppieters tells their mission. They carried the Gospel to the nations. Their tombs crown the Christian world. The foundation stones of the Church. Their names grace the calendar's feasts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-chu: A 1913 entry on the apostolic churches — the sees founded by apostles. Honoré Coppieters lists their proud claims. Rome, Antioch, and Alexandria lead. Their witness anchors the tradition. The mother churches of the world. Their bishops claim the ancient thrones. Their lists are the historians' treasure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-ind: A 1913 entry on apostolic indulgences — the favors attached to sacred objects. William Kent explains their use. The pope blesses rosaries and medals. The faithful gain the Church's treasury. The small print of the spiritual favors. Their list fills the Raccolta's pages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-argyll-and-th: This 1913 reference article on Argyll and the Isles — the Highland diocese. Oswald Hunter-Blair tells its island story. Its bishops serve the Gaelic glens. The Hebrides keep the old faith. Scotland's western bishopric. Its Iona abbey crowns the holy isle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aristides: This 1913 reference article on Aristides — the Athenian apologist. Edward Pace honors his ancient Apology. His defense reached Hadrian's court. The Armenian version saved his text. A philosopher turned Christian. His apology is the Christians' earliest. His text survives in Syriac dress.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ashes: A 1913 entry on ashes in the liturgy — the symbol of penance and mourning. Herbert Thurston surveys their sacred use. The palms of last year feed the fire. The faithful wear the ancient sign. The dust of the Church's sorrow. Their blessing opens the Lenten rite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asperges: A 1913 entry on the Asperges — the Sunday sprinkling with holy water. John Wynne explains its cleansing rite. Thou shalt sprinkle me, the choir sings. The people are signed before Mass. The week's fresh purification. Its hyssop was the ancient sprinkler.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-attaliates: This 1913 reference piece on Michael Attaleiates — the Byzantine historian. Thomas Shahan notes his chronicle. His pages lit the eleventh century. The entry preserves his modest fame. A lawyer among historians. His Diataxis ordered the poorhouse. His history ends with Botaneiates' fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-autos-sacrame: This 1913 reference article on the autos sacramentales — Spain's Corpus Christi plays. Ventura Fuentes honors their sacred drama. Calderón crowned the lofty form. The crowds learned the Eucharist's praise. The theater of the Blessed Sacrament. Their stages filled the Corpus squares.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auxilius-of-n: This 1913 reference piece on Auxilius of Naples — the defender of Pope Formosus. Johann Peter Kirsch honors his brave pen. His tracts answered the cadaver synod. The ninth century heard his plea. A priest against the powerful. His Libellus defended the dead pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-averroes: This 1913 reference piece on Averroes — the Commentator of Cordoba. William Turner weighs his fateful influence. His Aristotle shook the medieval schools. St. Thomas answered his errors. The most famous Arab philosopher. His tomb lies in Moroccan earth. His commentaries filled the schoolmen's desks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-azores: This 1913 reference article on the Azores — the mid-Atlantic islands' church story. Ewan Macpherson gives its island tale. The settlers brought their parish priests. The Holy Ghost feasts crown the year. A diocese of the ocean isles. Their tea grows on Sao Miguel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-azymes: A 1913 entry on azymes — the unleavened bread of the Passover. Francis Albert explains its scriptural use. The Latins bake the host unleavened. The Greeks keep the leavened loaf. The bread of the ancient feast. Their use is the Latin custom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-azymites: This 1913 reference article on the Azymites — the Greeks' name for the unleavened Latins. James Loughlin tells the old quarrel. The bread of the Eucharist divided East and West. The schism fed on such points. A nickname of the great divide.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balearic-isle: A 1913 entry on the Balearic Isles — Majorca, Minorca, and Iviza. Joseph Lins tells their church story. The Catalans brought the faith. The island sees guard the old rites. A diocese of the western sea. Their slingers were Rome's terror. Their cathedrals crown the island hills.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baptistines: This 1913 reference article on the Baptistines — a religious family of note. Jean Besse records their modest story. The entry preserves their humble fame. Their work serves the Church's need. A congregation of the faithful. Their habit marks the cloistered life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bardesanes-an: This 1913 reference article on Bardesanes — the Syriac gnostic of Edessa. John Arendzen tells his strange tale. His hymns charmed the eastern Church. The Fathers refuted his errors. A heretic with a poet's soul. His Book of the Laws survives. His son carried on the sect.

Paul Foster Case, an American occultist and founder of the Builders of the Adytum, wrote The Great Seal of the United States. His subject is the history, symbolism, and message of the national emblem. Case read public symbols as carriers of hidden teaching. The Great Seal, with its pyramid and eye, drew him strongly.

He traces the seal's making in the 1780s and reads its parts: the eagle, the shield, the unfinished pyramid, and the Latin mottos Annuit Coeptis and Novus Ordo Seclorum. For Case the seal announces a new age for mankind. The book decodes the nation's emblem for readers of his school, in the archive's collection.
govdocs-archive_org-SpanishUFOFiles_Span:

The papers cover sightings brought to official attention and the inquiries that followed, recorded in the dry language of state paperwork. Read together, they show how a modern government handled reports it could not easily explain. For UFO researchers, official releases like these matter because they rest on documents rather than retellings, and claims can be checked against the record.
govdocs-archive_org-TheFBIAndCISPES_The_:

The inquiry, from the 101st Congress, reviewed how the Bureau had treated an American group opposed to United States policy in Central America.

The report sets out what the FBI did, on whose authority, and where the committee found fault with the investigation. It became part of the wider record of 1980s fights over domestic surveillance of political groups. Readers get Congress's own oversight findings, drawn from the Bureau's files and testimony.
govdocs-archive_org-Volume3Part2HowHelpC:

Agents were looking for any record of James Earl Ray or his associates at the motel, and the check found none. Negative results fill much of the MURKIN file, because proving where Ray had not been mattered to a case built on his movements. The single teletype is preserved as issued, one page of the Bureau's legwork.

podcast-joerogan-RB-O0V9djEs:

hinton-scientific-romances-first-series:
Charles Howard Hinton, a British mathematician, issued his Scientific Romances in essays between 1884 and 1886. Hinton coined the word 'tesseract' for a four-dimensional cube. His tales were the first great push to make the fourth dimension known to general readers.

The essays mix story and study: flat worlds, beings who pass through solid walls, and drills for picturing four dimensions. Hinton thought training the mind to see past three dimensions could free it. His work fed later writers of higher-space fiction, and Abbott's Flatland appeared in the same years.
boethius-consolation-philosophy-james:
Boethius, a Roman senator and scholar, wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison in 524, awaiting execution under King Theodoric. H. R. James's English translation is the text here. Boethius had been the king's chief minister; now, stripped of office and wealth, he wrote his way toward calm.

Lady Philosophy visits his cell and talks him out of self-pity, step by step. She shows that fortune's gifts were never truly his, and that the good cannot be taken by force. The famous wheel of fortune turns through the book. Verse and prose trade places as the argument climbs. It was among the most loved books of the Middle Ages.
joinville-memoirs-st-louis-johnes:
Jean de Joinville, a French knight, finished his Memoirs of Louis IX in 1309, nearly sixty years after the events. Thomas Johnes's English translation is the text here, from Bohn's Chronicles of the Crusades. Joinville sailed with King Louis on the Seventh Crusade and knew him as a friend.

The memoir mixes the king's holy sayings and just deeds with Joinville's own adventures in Egypt: battles on the Nile, captivity after Mansourah, and ransom talks. Louis appears praying, judging under an oak, and washing the feet of the poor. The book is the most intimate life of any medieval king. Its appendix adds knight lists and a Saracen account of the crusade.
asser-life-king-alfred-giles:
Asser, a Welsh monk from St David's, wrote his Life of King Alfred in 893, during the king's lifetime. J. A. Giles's English translation is the text here, from his Six Old English Chronicles. Asser had joined Alfred's court in 885 and wrote as a friend and daily companion.

The life mixes a chronicle of the Viking wars with intimate detail: Alfred's childhood, his illnesses, his hunger for learning, and his program of translating Latin books into English. Asser shows the king dividing his income and his hours with a monk's exactness. It is the first biography of an English king by a man who knew him. Its authenticity has been debated; its charm has not.
geoffrey-monmouth-history-kings-britain-:
Geoffrey of Monmouth completed his History of the Kings of Britain around 1136, and it became a medieval bestseller. J. A. Giles's translation is the text here, from his Six Old English Chronicles. Geoffrey claimed to translate a very ancient book in the British tongue. What he really did was invent much of Britain's past.

From Brutus of Troy, his kings run through Lear, Cymbeline, and the long line to Arthur, whose reign fills the book's center. Merlin's prophecies thread the story. Shakespeare drew Lear and Cymbeline from Geoffrey's pages, and Arthur's world starts here. Historians scolded the book for centuries while everyone read it. It is myth-making of the first order.
nsa-manhattan-project-director-files:
In 2024 the National Security Archive published this Nuclear Vault briefing book from the files of General Leslie Groves, director of the Manhattan Project. The declassified documents open a window on the atomic bomb's early history. Groves ran the project from 1942 with near-total power and a passion for secrecy.

The papers cover the project's organization, its vast sites and security web, and the choices that led to the Trinity test of July 1945. Letters and memos show Groves settling fights over science, labor, and spies. The briefing shows how one office steered the largest secret enterprise of the war. The documents are United States government records.
baring-gould-curious-myths-1867-second-s:
Sabine Baring-Gould, a Devon priest with a vast store of lore, made this second set of his Curious Myths in 1867. The text here is the 1868 print. He dealt with the odd tales of the Middle Ages and sought their roots.

One long part traces the tale of Melusina, the fairy bride, from land to land. Swan maids and the Fortunate Isles, the isles of the blest in the west sea, fill other parts. The set was the main Victorian guide to such tales, read far past its own age.
hunt-popular-romances-west-england-1865-:
Robert Hunt, a Cornish man of science, made this first set of the folk tales of the west of England in 1865. He heard most of the tales in Cornwall, from miners, fish wives, and old folk. His aim was to save the lore of old Cornwall before it died out.

The set holds the famed tale of the Mermaid of Zennor, who lured a choir man to the sea. Giants, saints, mine sprites, and strange dreams fill the rest of the Cornish store. Hunt's work is the chief book of the folk lore of the Cornish coast.

Robert Hunt brought out the second set of his Cornish folk tales in 1865, in the Hotten print of that year. It stands as mate to the first set of the same year. Hunt spent years in the lanes and ports of Cornwall to gather his store.

More drolls, as Cornish folk name their sly tales, fill this set with fresh lore. Saints, giants, sea tales, and old rites of the Cornish year all find a place here. With the first set, it forms the full record of old Cornwall as its folk told it.
grim-tales:
E. Nesbit was famed for bright tales for young readers, such as her books of child quests. In 1893 she showed a far more dark face in this set of horror tales. The change shocked some fans who knew just the gay side of her pen.

The best known tale, 'Man-Size in Marble,' turns on two stone knights in a church who may not stay still. Dread in wed life, in homes, and in love runs through the set as its core theme. The set is the dark twin of her famed books for the young.
king-solomons-mines:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this adventure tale in a rush of work in 1885, to match a bet on the style of Treasure Island. It was his first big hit, and it made his name at a stroke. Allan Quatermain, a dry and tough hunter, tells the tale in his own voice.

Quatermain leads two English men deep in Africa to find the lost mines of King Solomon. Maps, deserts, a lost tribe, and a vast hoard of gems fill the road there and back. The book made the lost world tale a set form for a hundred years of thrills.
phantastes:
George MacDonald, a Scots priest and poet, wrote this first of his great tales in 1858. He was then a young man, and the book broke new ground at a stroke. It tells of Anodos, a youth of one and twenty years, on the day he comes of age.

Anodos finds a gate in his room to Fairy Land and walks its woods and streams. Maids of ash and alder, a knight, and a dark shade mark his road of growth and loss. The book is the first great fantasy of the Victorian age, and it shaped C. S. Lewis.
the-captain-of-the-pole-star-and-other-t:
Arthur Conan Doyle made this set of his weird tales in 1890, and it here stands in the text of the Longmans print. The set bears the name of its first tale, of a ghost ship in the polar seas. Doyle was then a young doctor, just at the start of his famed life as a writer.

Arctic ghosts walk in 'The Captain of the Pole-Star,' told as a ship's log in the ice. 'J. Habakuk Jephson's Statement' gives a ghost ship's tale, and 'The Ring of Thoth' an Egyptian one. The set holds the best of Doyle's tales of the unseen from his first years.
gildas-on-the-ruin-of-britain-giles:
Gildas, a British monk of the sixth century, wrote On the Ruin of Britain as a sermon of blame against his own kings and priests. J. A. Giles translated the Latin for the modern reader. The work is the only connected narrative source for Britain after the Romans left. Everything else for those years is scraps and saints' tales.

Gildas tells of Roman rule, the coming of the Saxons as hired swords, their revolt, and the wars of Ambrosius and the siege of Badon. Then he turns on the five kings of his day and scourges their sins. His Latin is hot, tangled, and full of scripture. Later ages mined him for Arthur's age, though he never names Arthur.
b09-luther-95theses:
Martin Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses on October 31, 1517, under the formal title Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences. An indulgence was a church grant that cut the penalty for sin, and its sale had grown into a trade. Luther, a monk and teacher at Wittenberg, wrote in Latin for debate among scholars.

The theses attack the sale point by point and deny that the pope can free souls from purgatory at will. Luther asks what true sorrow for sin is worth next to a bought pardon. Few short texts have changed so much: this one lit the spark of the Reformation. It remains the most cited single document of that break.
b09-melanchthon-loci-communes:
Philipp Melanchthon was only twenty-four when his Loci Communes appeared in 1521. The Latin title means commonplaces, the main topics of theology set in order. No one had yet given the young Reformation a full, ordered system of teaching, and this book did it first.

Melanchthon builds the system straight from Paul's letter to the Romans, topic by topic. Sin, law, grace, and faith stand at the center of the scheme. The Latin text here follows the first form of the work, in the edition of G L Plitt as revised by Th Kolde. Students of the Reformation still treat it as the movement's first dogmatics.
keckley-behind-the-scenes:
Elizabeth Keckley published Behind the Scenes in 1868, with a subtitle that sums her life: thirty years a slave, four years in the White House. Keckley bought her freedom with her needle, then became Mary Todd Lincoln's dressmaker. She was also the First Lady's closest confidante.

She tells of slavery in Virginia and North Carolina, her son's death in Union uniform, and the Lincoln household at war. Lincoln's assassination and his widow's grief fill the closing chapters. The book caused a scandal for its private details. Today it is prized as a rare insider view of the Civil War White House.
galton-memories:
Francis Galton published Memories of My Life in 1908, summing up one of the most varied careers in Victorian science. Galton was Darwin's cousin, and his interests seemed endless. Travel, weather, heredity, and measurement all drew his restless mind.

He recalls exploring in southwest Africa, mapping weather patterns, and inventing the fingerprint method for identification. His work on heredity and human ability, which he named eugenics, fills later chapters and now draws sharp criticism. Galton writes with dry humor about his many failures and fixes. The memoir shows the making of modern statistics, for better and for worse.
rockefeller-reminiscences:
John Rockefeller published his Random Reminiscences of Men and Events in 1909. The founder of Standard Oil was then the first billionaire in American history. Critics expected a defense; instead he offered calm reflections on business and giving.

Rockefeller tells of his start as a bookkeeper, his early oil ventures, and the building of a vast company. He shares his rules: keep accounts, respect partners, and give while you live. Friends, rivals, and church life appear between the business chapters. The book is short and guarded, yet it remains the richest American of his age speaking in his own words.
douglass-life-and-times:
Life and Times of Frederick Douglass, first published in 1881 and revised in 1892, is his third and fullest autobiography. Douglass had become a statesman of Reconstruction, a marshal, a diplomat, and the leading Black voice in America. This is the capstone of his life's writing.

He retells his enslavement and escape, then follows his public career through the Civil War and beyond. His meetings with Lincoln, his recruiting of Black troops, and his posts in Washington fill the second half. Douglass looks back with pride and continued fight. The book completes the greatest life story written by an American born enslaved.
willard-glimpses:
Frances Willard published Glimpses of Fifty Years in 1889, her autobiography and the story of a movement. Willard led the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, the largest women's group in America. Her pen name for the cause was 'Home Protection.'

She tells of her Illinois girlhood, teaching, and grief at her brother's death, which turned her to reform. Under her lead the temperance fight joined suffrage, labor, and prison reform. Her famous tale of learning to ride a bicycle at fifty-three symbolizes her push for women's freedom. The book blends memoir, speeches, and the record of a vast campaign.
winnemucca-life-among-piutes:
Sarah Winnemucca Hopkins published Life Among the Piutes in 1883, the first autobiography by a Native American woman. Winnemucca, a Paiute interpreter and teacher, wrote in English for white readers whose help she sought. The book is both a life story and an indictment.

She tells of her grandfather Truckee's friendship with whites, her schooling in California, and her work as an interpreter. Then she charges reservation agents with theft, hunger, and broken promises to her people. Her account of the Bannock War pleads the Paiute case. Few nineteenth-century books speak so directly from inside a Native nation.
carlyle-reminiscences:
Thomas Carlyle, the Sage of Chelsea, wrote his Reminiscences in bursts of grief right after his wife's death in 1866. His friend and biographer James Froude published them in 1881. The pieces were never meant as a finished book, which gives them their raw force.

Carlyle recalls his father, his early friend Edward Irving, and the Scotland of his youth, now vanished. He writes of London fame and of Jane Welsh Carlyle with love and regret. The prose is tender, gloomy, and vivid by turns. Publication stirred scandal, since Carlyle spared neither himself nor others in these pages.
zola-four-short-stories:
Four short tales by Zola gather in this 1906 volume of his briefer fiction. Zola is best known for huge novels and a twenty-volume family saga. Here his range shows in a far smaller frame, tale by tale.

Love, war, country life, and Paris streets pass in a few vivid pages each. Compression suits him: scenes strike fast and leave a lasting mark. New readers often fear the scale of the Rougon-Macquart set. For them, these stories offer the easiest door into his world. They prove that the master of the vast canvas could also cut a gem in miniature, with the same clear eye.
zweig-jeremiah-a-drama-in-nine-scenes:
The prophet Jeremiah warns Jerusalem not to resist Babylon and gets condemned as a traitor for preaching peace. Stefan Zweig's Jeremiah, a drama in nine scenes from 1917, appears here in English. Written while the First World War raged, the play turns scripture into protest against the madness of nations.

Jeremiah's warnings fail, the city falls, and yet the prophet's vision of a renewed people survives the ruins. Zweig poured his own horror at the war into the ancient story. Nine powerful scenes move from court intrigue to exile's road. The drama stands as his most passionate public statement of the war years. It also launched his European fame as a writer of conscience.
derzhavin-spiritual-odes:
Russia's great eighteenth-century poet Gavrila Derzhavin speaks in his Spiritual Odes, given here in Russian. Derzhavin bridged classicism and the age of Pushkin, serving empresses while writing verse of startling personal force. His famous ode God stands among the landmarks of Russian poetry, translated across Europe in his lifetime.

Odes to God and meditations on death combine lofty philosophy with sudden, intimate feeling. A courtier who had seen favor and disgrace alike, Derzhavin writes about power's vanity from inside the palace. The Russian text preserves his bold, uneven music exactly. Modern Russian poetry effectively begins on this foundation stone. Readers with Russian will find the odes grand, strange, and unexpectedly tender.
korolenko-birds-of-heaven-and-other-stor:
Exiles, wanderers, and ordinary people enduring great hardship fill Birds of Heaven and Other Stories by Vladimir Korolenko, in English. Korolenko wrote as the humane conscience of Russian literature, and Chekhov counted him a favorite among living writers. Siberian roads and steppe villages supply most of the settings in this selection.

His tales observe convicts, pilgrims, and peasants with moral clarity and steady sympathy. No character is too small for his full attention, a quality readers noticed at once. The title story lifts its eyes from hard lives to the birds passing over them. Together the stories show why contemporaries trusted Korolenko's judgment on Russia itself. His kindness on the page was earned in a life of exile and advocacy.
korolenko-makar-s-dream-and-other-storie:
A Siberian peasant dies drunk before Christmas and argues his case in heaven in Korolenko's famous tale Makar's Dream, which heads this English collection. Makar, a poor dreamer cheated by life and by the local powers, pleads before the Great Toyon with peasant cunning. His scales of sins and good deeds produce the story's famous, tender verdict.

Funny, moving, and profound at once, the tale ranks among the great Russian short stories. Other pieces in the volume carry Korolenko's Siberian exile experience into fiction. He knew the taiga settlements he describes from years of banishment there. The collection makes a perfect doorway into his work. Few writers judge their characters so justly and forgive them so much.
bryusov-the-republic-of-the-southern-cro:
A polar republic dies of a mysterious disease of contradiction in the title story of Valery Bryusov's story collection, given here in English. Bryusov led the Russian Symbolists, and his tales mix utopias, plagues, and the occult with decadent polish. Madness spreads through a perfectly planned Antarctic city like a logical infection.

Other stories in the set range across history and fantasy with the same stylish control. Bryusov wrote prose the way his movement wrote verse: dense, musical, and deliberately strange. English readers meet a side of Russian fiction far from the great realist novels. The collection shows symbolism attempting the short story with full ambition. Strange and unlike anything else of its period, it rewards adventurous readers.
sologub-the-old-house-and-other-tales:
Fyodor Sologub wrote short tales of fear, decay, and strange beauty, and English readers meet them here in translation. He was a leading Russian Symbolist, a writer drawn to dark and uncanny moods. Schoolrooms, homes, and quiet streets become uneasy places in his hands.

Horror in these stories rarely comes from monsters or gore. It grows out of cruel adults, trapped children, and minds that twist small harms into grand terrors. Sologub mixes pity with dread and finds a cold beauty in rot and failure. Readers who want Symbolist fiction at its darkest will find his voice sharp, elegant, and hard to forget.
heckewelder-lenape-dialogues:
Words, Phrases, and Short Dialogues in the Lenape tongue appeared in 1819. Heckewelder gathered the material at Moravian stations on the frontier. Missionaries there had to preach and teach in the people's own language.

Word lists give the core terms of daily Lenape life and speech. Useful phrases cover travel, trade, food, and greetings between strangers. Short talks between speakers show the tongue in real use. The slim book was a working tool, not a work of show. Today it keeps early Lenape speech on record for new students of the tongue. Linguists still value its plain, field-gathered forms and phrases.
wieger-histoire-croyances:
Léon Wieger, a Jesuit sinologist in China, wrote his great survey in French in 1922. His History of Religious Beliefs and Philosophical Opinions covers all China. Confucian thought, Taoism, Buddhism, and the hundred schools fill its span.

Wieger spent his life among Chinese texts and Chinese teachers alike. He traces each school's birth, growth, and clash with its rivals. Dates, names, and key texts anchor his vast, ordered narrative. French readers treated the work as their standard guide for years. Few single books map two thousand years of Chinese thought so fully in French. Wieger's charts and lists help readers hold the vast span together.
wieger-textes-philosophiques:
Wieger's Textes philosophiques, in French from 1906, gathers the sources themselves. Chinese thinkers speak here in the Jesuit scholar's lucid French versions. Confucius, Laozi, and Zhuangzi lead a cast of lesser masters.

Short texts let readers test the claims of Wieger's great history. The wells from which that history drew stand open in this book. Moral maxims sit beside wild tales of sages who scorn all rule. Wieger picks and renders with a teacher's care for the new reader. The volume remains a fine first path into Chinese thought in French dress. Its short pieces suit readers new to the sages and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moab-moabites: The Moabites were Israel's neighbors across the Jordan, the people of Ruth and of King Mesha's famous victory stone. This entry covers their history, their land, and their tangled relations with Israel. The cousins across the river: their story runs through Ruth, David, and the prophets.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mohammedan-co: The Sufi brotherhoods are Islam's mystical orders, and this entry surveys their founders, their practices, and their place in Muslim life. A Catholic scholar's guide to Islamic mysticism. The dervishes, explained: their orders shaped Muslim piety from Senegal to Indonesia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monothelitism: The Monothelites taught that Christ has only one will, and the Sixth Ecumenical Council condemned them in 681. This entry explains the doctrine, its imperial patrons, and its defeat. The last great Christological heresy: its defeat completed the Church's doctrine of Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monterey-and-: The archdiocese of Monterey and Los Angeles carried California's Catholic story from the Spanish missions to the American metropolis. This entry covers its bishops, from the mission era to 1913, and its parishes. The Church of the Golden State: its missions founded the cities of coastal California.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moses: Moses led Israel out of Egypt, received the Law on Sinai, and became the Bible's greatest prophet. This long entry covers his biblical story, the questions of the higher critics, and his place in Jewish and Christian tradition. The lawgiver, examined from every side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-of-beat: The Mount of Beatitudes overlooks the Sea of Galilee where tradition places the Sermon on the Mount. This entry covers its site, its church, and the Beatitudes themselves. The hill of the happiest sermon ever preached: its church honors the eight Beatitudes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-musical-instr: Should the organ play in church? This entry traces the debate over musical instruments in worship, from the early Church's a cappella ideal to the organ's triumph. The long argument over God's soundtrack: the entry traces organs from suspicion to glory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nahanes: The Nahane peoples of British Columbia's northern interior hunted the mountain valleys little touched by the outside world. This entry by Adrian Morice notes their territory, customs, and mission history. Life in the northern ranges: their hunting grounds stretched across the Stikine country.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nantes: Nantes is famous for the Edict of 1598 that gave French Protestants toleration, revoked by Louis XIV in 1685. This entry covers its diocese, its bishops, and its history. The city of the edict and its revocation: its cathedral witnessed both triumph and tragedy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-naples: Naples, the great city of the bay, has been an archbishop's see since the early Church, guarded by the blood of St. Januarius. This entry covers its archdiocese, its churches, and its vibrant Catholic life. The faith in the shadow of Vesuvius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-natchitoches: Natchitoches, the oldest town in Louisiana, became a diocese serving the state's Catholic north. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The faith in the land of Cane River: French Creoles built its first parishes along the Red River.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nathinites: The Nethinim were the temple servants of ancient Israel, given to the Levites for the sanctuary's menial work. This entry explains their origin, their duties, and their place in the biblical record. The humblest servants of the house of God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-necrologies: Necrologies are the monasteries' books of the dead, recording each brother's passing for prayer and memory. This entry explains their history, their form, and their value to historians. The community's roll of the departed: their names were read aloud on anniversaries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-hebrides: The New Hebrides, now Vanuatu, received Marist and other missionaries among their Melanesian peoples in the 1800s. This entry covers the islands, the missions, and the vicariate. The Church in the South Pacific's archipelago: its missions served eighty island languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nikolaus-nill: This biographical entry profiles Nikolaus Nilles, an Austrian Jesuit liturgist of the 1800s, tracing his career, his studies of Eastern rites, and his scholarship as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Jesuit gallery, preserved among its records of Austrian liturgists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nimes: Nîmes, the Roman city of the Maison Carrée and the arena, has been a bishop's see since the early Church. This entry covers its diocese, its bishops, and its history. Antiquity and faith in the Gard: its Roman arena still hosts the crowds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notaries: Notaries are the Church's official record-keepers, and this entry explains their ancient history, their appointment, and their duties in canon law. The scribes of ecclesiastical justice: their signatures and seals authenticate every official act of the diocese and its tribunal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notre-dame-de: This entry profiles a Marian shrine of early French Canada, tracing its foundation, its pilgrims, and its place in the devotional life of New France as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact sketch from the encyclopedia's Canadian gallery, preserved among its records of New France's shrines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nueva-caceres: Nueva Cáceres, now Naga City, became the great archdiocese of the Bicol region in the Philippines. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The faith in the land of the Virgin of Peñafrancia: its cathedral serves the Bicolanos of the Philippines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-obedientiarie: Obedientiaries were the monastery's officers, from cellarer to sacristan, each with his defined charge. This entry explains their offices, their duties, and their history. The abbey's chain of command: their titles survive in modern monasteries to this very day unchanged.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oblates-of-sa: The Oblates of St. Francis de Sales were founded to live the gentle saint's spirit in preaching and education. This entry covers their foundation, their work, and their growth. The spirit of de Sales, in a congregation: their schools spread across three continents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orate-fratres: Orate Fratres is the priest's appeal at the Offertory: pray, brethren, that my sacrifice and yours may be acceptable. This entry explains its text, its history, and its meaning. The people's Amen to the offering: the Suscipiat answers the priest's plea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-gilb: The Gilbertines were England's only native monastic order, founded by St. Gilbert of Sempringham for both men and women. This entry traces their foundation, their houses, and their suppression. England's own order: its double houses sheltered both sexes in prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-serv: The Servites were founded by the Seven Holy Founders of Florence in 1233 to serve Our Lady. This entry traces their foundation, their saints, and their worldwide work. The servants of Mary: their black habit honors the sorrows of Our Lady.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orientation-o: Churches face east toward the rising sun, the symbol of Christ. This entry explains the custom's history, its symbolism, and its exceptions. Why altars look to the dawn: the entry traces the ancient custom all the way back to the apostles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orphans-and-o: Orphans and orphanages are the Church's immemorial charity, from the early Church's widows to the great institutions of the 1800s. This entry surveys their history and the orders that serve them. The Church as mother to the motherless: their homes sheltered thousands of children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osorio-franci: This biographical entry profiles Osorio Francisco Meneses, a Spanish painter of the Baroque era, tracing his career, his works, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's artistic gallery, preserved among its records of Spanish painters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-overpopulatio: Overpopulation theories from Malthus onward warned that mankind would outgrow its food. This entry by John Ryan examines the theories, their errors, and the Catholic view. The dismal science, answered: Ryan refuted Malthus with the moral tools of Catholic economics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parables: The parables are Jesus's incomparable stories, from the sower to the prodigal son. This long entry examines their nature, their interpretation, and their theology. The master storyteller's art: their deep meanings unfold only for the truly humble and pure of heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paralipomenon: Paralipomenon, or Chronicles, retells Israel's story from Adam to the exile with a priestly eye. This entry examines its books, their authorship, and their theology. The Bible's second telling: its long genealogies trace the promised royal line of great David.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passion-offic: The Passion Offices are the Holy Week liturgies that walk with Christ to Calvary. This entry explains their structure, their chants, and their history. The week's solemn journey: their solemn Tenebrae slowly shroud the darkened church in deepening gathering darkness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patriarchate-: The Patriarchate of the East Indies was the proud title of the archbishops of Goa, primates of the East. This entry traces its history, its claims, and its jurisdiction. The Rome of the East: its cathedral witnessed the Portuguese empire's glory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peace-congres: Peace congresses were the 1800s gatherings that dreamed of ending war by arbitration. This entry surveys their history, their achievements, and the Catholic view. The dream of perpetual peace: their Hague conferences built the world's first permanent courts of arbitration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-augusti: Bishop Peter Baines was the vicar-apostolic who governed the Western District of England in the 1800s. This entry traces his career, his colleges, and his administration. The bishop of the old west country: his Downside connections shaped the whole district.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pharisees: The Pharisees were the Jewish party of the law whose disputes with Christ fill the Gospels. This entry explains their doctrines, their history, and their legacy. The separated ones of Israel: their fierce zeal for the law shaped later Judaism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippe-de-c: Philippe de Commines was the chronicler whose memoirs of Louis XI founded modern political history. This entry covers his career, his memoirs, and his wisdom. The father of modern memoirs: his shrewd pages unmasked the wily spider king of France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philistines: The Philistines were the sea peoples who warred with Israel from their five cities. This entry explains their origins, their wars, and their fate. The giants' kin of the coastal plain: their champion Goliath fell to young David's sling and stone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-phylacteries: Phylacteries are the little leather boxes of Scripture that observant Jews bind to forehead and arm. This entry explains their form, their texts, and their meaning. The frontlets of the law: their dark straps bind the Shema to the body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-picture-bible: Picture Bibles were the illustrated Scriptures that taught the illiterate Middle Ages. This entry traces their forms, from the Biblia Pauperum to the block books, and their beauty. The Gospel in images: their vivid woodcuts taught the wondering ploughman his Creed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-puvis-: Puvis de Chavannes was the muralist whose pale frescoes adorned the Panthéon and the Sorbonne. This entry covers his career, his works, and his influence. The painter of the serene wall: his calm figures float serenely above the troubled real.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pilgrimages: Pilgrimages are the sacred journeys that have drawn the faithful to holy places in every age. This entry traces their history, their shrines, and their spirit. The road to the holy places: its great shrines span every continent on earth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poles-in-the-: The Poles in America built the churches and parishes of the great immigration. This entry traces their settlements, their parishes, and their institutions. The faith of the emigrant millions: their sturdy parishes dotted the great industrial cities of the East.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polyglot-bibl: Polyglot Bibles are the great multilingual editions from Complutum to Paris. This entry traces their editors, their texts, and their scholarship. The Scriptures in many tongues: their stately columns aligned Hebrew, Greek, and Latin side by side in printed glory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontifical-au: Pontifical audiences are the pope's formal receptions of pilgrims, princes, and prelates. This entry explains their kinds, their ceremonial, and their meaning. The face-to-face with Peter's successor: their ancient protocol guards the sacred papal dignity of eternal Rome itself in splendor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontifical-co: The pontifical colleges are Rome's national seminaries, training priests for the whole world. This entry surveys their foundations, their students, and their work. The nurseries of the universal Church: their learned alumni lead the Catholic nations of the whole earth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poor-clares: The Poor Clares are St. Clare's daughters, the first Franciscan nuns. This entry traces their foundation, their rule, and their spread. The enclosed lilies of Assisi: their holy silence preaches louder to the noisy world outside their high convent walls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-milti: Miltiades was the saintly pope who saw Constantine's victory dawn. This entry traces his pontificate, the Lateran's gift, and his veneration. The pope of the Milvian Bridge's year: his gifted Lateran housed the popes for a thousand years and more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portraits-of-: The portraits of the apostles are the earliest Christian images, from catacombs to mosaics. This entry traces their types, their symbols, and their history. The faces of the Twelve in art: their venerable types are ancient indeed in Christian art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-preadamites: The Preadamites theory imagined men before Adam. This entry examines the claim, its refutations, and the Catholic teaching. The men who never were: their strange theory troubled the orthodox theologians of olden times greatly indeed in learned debate halls everywhere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-protectories: Protectories were the Catholic reformatories for wayward youth. This entry notes their foundation, their methods, and their success. The homes of the rescued child: their busy workshops trained the young hands for honest trades and Christian lives of labor and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-protestant-ep: The Protestant Episcopal Church is America's Anglican communion. This entry traces its bishops, its prayer book, and its history. The church of the colonial establishment: its first bishops came from England's shores in 1787's cold winter of newfound freedom and peace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-purgatorial-s: Purgatorial societies are the confraternities that pray for the dead. This entry notes their foundation, their works, and their spread. The leagues of the holy souls: their offered Masses hasten the souls' release from purgatorial pain and holy fire in mercy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quarantines: Quarantines are the forty-day periods of prayer and indulgence. This entry explains their origin, their observance, and their grants. The forty days of devotion: their rich indulgences enriched the pious faithful in Lent's long days of prayer and fast and alms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ralph-baines: Ralph Baines was the Hebrew scholar and bishop of Coventry. This entry notes his works, his exile, and his loyalty. The bishop of Mary's reign: his pure Hebrew graced the Paris schools of olden days gone by in lecture and in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raphael-semme: Raphael Semmes was the Confederate admiral of the Alabama. This entry traces his cruises, his victories, and his memoirs. The sea-wolf of the South: his swift Alabama terrorized the Union seas in 1863's bright summer months of war and blockade.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-d-agi: Raymond d'Agiles was the chaplain-chronicler of the First Crusade. This entry notes his history, its value, and its legends. The priest of the crusaders' march: his faithful pen recorded the great siege of Antioch in 1098's cold winter of hunger.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rechab-and-th: Rechab and the Rechabites were the austere clan of the desert. This entry treats their vow, their fidelity, and their blessing. The teetotalers of the Old Testament: their stern vow pleased the prophet Jeremiah in Judah's rocky hills of old.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-redemptoristi: The Redemptoristines are St. Alphonsus's contemplative nuns. This entry traces their foundation, their rule, and their houses. The brides of the Redeemer: their silent cloister hides the busy world outside its high walls in Scala's green hills of Italy forever.

the-happy-prince-and-other-tales: Oscar Wilde's 1888 fairy tales, including "The Happy Prince," "The Nightingale and the Rose," and "The Selfish Giant." sketches-of-young-couples: Dickens's comic gallery of engaged and newly married couples, from the blissful to the bickering. Written in 1840 with illustrator Phiz, these short character sketches show his early gift for catching human folly in a few strokes. Light, affectionate, and very funny.
tom-swift-and-his-big-tunnel-or-the-hidd: Tom Swift blasts a tunnel through the Andes and discovers a hidden city in this 1916 adventure. uncle-josh-s-punkin-centre-stories: Cal Stewart's vaudeville tales of Uncle Josh Weathersby, the drawling New England farmer whose "punkin centre" stories delighted millions on phonograph records. the-water-babies: Charles Kingsley's 1863 fantasy about Tom, a chimney-sweep boy who becomes a "water-baby" and learns morality among the fishes. Part fairy tale, part sermon on cleanliness and kindness, and part satire on Victorian science, it charmed and preached to generations. Dated in places but full of inventive wonder.
joe-wilson-and-his-mates: Stories by Henry Lawson, Australia's beloved bush writer, about Joe Wilson, a swagman drifting through the outback. moon-face-and-other-stories: Jack London's 1906 collection, named for the title story of a man who schemes to kill a neighbor he hates on sight. The other tales roam from the Yukon to the South Seas, all in London's muscular style. Strong, strange, and sometimes cruel, they show the author of The Call of the Wild at his most intense.
the-itinerary-of-archbishop-baldwin-thro: Gerald of Wales's 1188 account of traveling through Wales with Archbishop Baldwin, preaching the Crusade. Vivid, gossipy, and learned, it describes Welsh customs, legends, and landscape with a medieval insider's eye. One of the great travel books of the Middle Ages.
the-description-of-wales: Gerald of Wales's companion to his Itinerary: a full account of the Welsh people, their laws, music, and character, written around 1194. Proud of his homeland, Gerald praises Welsh courage and poetry while noting their faults. A landmark of medieval ethnography, lively and opinionated.
war-of-the-classes: Jack London's 1905 essays preaching socialism to American workers. Fiery, idealistic, and combative, they show the other London: not just the adventure writer but the committed revolutionary. A fascinating window into the radical politics of the Progressive Era.
south-sea-tales: Jack London's stories of the South Pacific: pearl divers, beachcombers, and traders living hard under the tropical sun. glasses: Henry James's 1896 story about a beautiful woman whose charm depends on no one knowing she is nearly blind. The narrator's fascination and the lady's secret build to a quietly devastating revelation. A small masterpiece about seeing and not seeing.
taras-bulba-and-other-tales: Gogol's epic of the Cossacks: old Taras Bulba and his sons ride to war against Poland in a tale of fierce loyalty and tragic betrayal. dolly-dialogues: Anthony Hope's 1894 drawing-room dialogues between the witty Dolly and her admirer, sparkling with epigrams on love, marriage, and society. Light, clever, and very much of the 1890s, they made Hope famous before The Prisoner of Zenda. Delightful period wit.
sesame-and-lilies: John Ruskin's famous 1865 lectures: "Of Kings' Treasuries" on the value of books and reading, and "Of Queens' Gardens" on women's education and influence. some-reminiscences: Joseph Conrad's 1912 memoir of his Polish childhood, his years at sea, and his turn to writing. Ironic, moving, and beautifully written, it explains the man behind the novels without ever quite explaining him. The essential companion to Conrad's fiction.
the-water-goats-and-other-troubles: Humor stories by Ellis Parker Butler, the "Pigs is Pigs" man, about ordinary Americans in absurd predicaments. Goats, neighbors, and small-town logic collide in tales of cheerful nonsense. Light, silly, and very funny, from a master of the comic short story.
three-ghost-stories: Dickens's supernatural trio: "The Signal-Man," "The Haunted House," and "The Trial for Murder," each a masterclass in dread. Railway ghosts, Christmas hauntings, and a murdered man who will not rest show Dickens's darker genius. Short, chilling, and perfect.
penelope-s-irish-experiences: Penelope's Irish tour: Kate Douglas Wiggin's bright American heroine takes on castles, jaunting cars, and the blarney of Ireland. the-collection-of-antiquities: Balzac's 1839 novel of provincial aristocrats clinging to the old order in post-Napoleonic France. The d'Esgrignon family fights a losing battle against bourgeois money and new ways. Ironic and elegiac, it is Balzac's farewell to the world of the old nobility.
the-garden-party-and-other-stories: Katherine Mansfield's 1922 collection, the high point of her art: "The Garden Party," "The Daughters of the Late Colonel," and other perfect stories of New Zealand and London life. the-jimmyjohn-boss-and-other-stories: Owen Wister's Western stories about the Jimmyjohn Boss and other frontier characters, told with his usual authenticity and charm. Cowboys, rustlers, and range life fill these tales from the author of The Virginian. Solid Western entertainment.
rienzi-the-last-of-the-roman-tribunes: Bulwer-Lytton's 1835 historical novel about Cola di Rienzi, who tried to restore the Roman republic in the 14th century. beacon-lights-of-history-volume-3-part-1: John Lord's popular 19th-century history lectures: this volume covers the Middle Ages, from Charlemagne to the Crusades. Written for general readers and students, it tells history through great lives. Old-fashioned but engaging popular history.
some-christmas-stories: A gathering of Dickens's Christmas writings: tales of the season from across his career, mixing ghosts, charity, and holiday cheer. The Christmas Carol's companions, full of the warmth that made Dickens the laureate of Christmas. Festive reading at its finest.
andersen-s-fairy-tales: The essential Hans Christian Andersen: "The Ugly Duckling," "The Little Mermaid," "The Emperor's New Clothes," "The Snow Queen," and more. Sad, strange, and beautiful, these Danish tales remade children's literature. The greatest fairy-tale writer after the Grimms.
charmides: In this dialogue Plato asks what it means to master oneself. old-english-libraries: Ernest Albert Savage's 1911 history of English libraries from medieval monasteries to the modern public library. Learned and enthusiastic, it traces how books were kept, chained, and shared. A treat for bibliophiles and historians of the book.
the-brick-moon-and-other-stories: Edward Everett Hale's 1869 collection led by "The Brick Moon," the first story ever written about an artificial satellite. A brick sphere launched as a navigation aid becomes humanity's first space station. Visionary science fiction, decades ahead of its time.
laches: Plato's dialogue on courage brings two Athenian generals to Socrates with a simple question: what is bravery? From the battlefield to the soul, each definition crumbles under his gentle questioning. No neat answer survives, but the search itself teaches. Socratic inquiry at its finest.
